Interviewer: "What's the difference between SNS and SQS? When do you use each one?"

SQS is a mailbox. Messages sit there until someone grabs them. Great when you need to queue up work, handle spiky traffic, or make sure nothing gets lost.

Key diff: SNS = push (send and forget). SQS = pull (grab when ready).

Example: Your app crashes. Use SNS to alert your team NOW. But if you need to process 10k orders today, throw them in SQS so workers can grab them one at a time without getting slammed.

Interviewer: "You're running containers in ECS. How do you keep your app safe from the internet?"

You use security groups. Think of them like a bouncer at a club. They say: "Yeah, traffic on port 80 can come in. Port 22? Nah, not today."

ECS containers run inside a VPC (your private network). By default, nothing from the internet can reach them. You only open the ports you need.

The setup:
- Create a security group for your ECS tasks
- Allow port 80/443 for web traffic (from anywhere)
- Block everything else
- Attach it to your load balancer in front

The load balancer sits in public. Your containers hide behind it and the security group.

Pro tip: Don't open port 22 (SSH) to 0.0.0.0. That's asking for trouble. Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager instead—it's way safer.

- You can rotate passwords without touching code

Interviewer: "Walk me through what happens when you configure a firewall rule. Why does order matter?"

ohh this trips people up


A firewall reads rules from top to bottom. It stops at the first match. So order = everything.

Example: You have two rules:
1. Block port 22 (SSH)
2. Allow port 22 from 10.0.0.0/8

If rule 1 is first? SSH gets blocked. Rule 2 never runs. You just locked yourself out.

Flip them? Now SSH works from your network. Good.

Pro tip: Put specific rules first (allow from this IP), then general rules (block everyone). Think of it like a bouncer checking a list. Check VIPs first, then run the general rules.

In AWS security groups or Linux iptables, same deal. Order matters big time.

Interviewer: "How do you pass config to a container in Kubernetes?"

This one's important. You've got 3 main ways:

1. ConfigMap — for regular stuff like app settings, db host, etc. Just key-value pairs. Not secret.

2. Secret — same idea but for passwords, api keys, stuff you don't want in plain text.

3. Environment variables — you point to ConfigMap or Secret and boom, your app reads them.

Here's the catch: if you change a ConfigMap, your pod doesn't auto-restart. You gotta manually restart it or use a tool like Sealed Secrets.

Real example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  DATABASE_HOST: postgres.default
  LOG_LEVEL: info
---
In your pod, mount it:
env:
  - name: DB_HOST
    valueFrom:
      configMapKeyRef:
        name: app-config
        key: DATABASE_HOST

The gotcha: ConfigMaps are NOT encrypted by default. Use Secrets for sensitive stuff.

#Kubernetes #DevOps #ContainerOrchestration #InterviewPrep

Big difference: Auto Scaling manages server groups. Karpenter manages individual pods.

Karpenter also picks cheaper servers that fit your needs. Auto Scaling just uses whatever you told it to use.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you handle pod crashes in Kubernetes?' — Most candidates say 'restart policies' and stop there. Here's what they miss 👇
thread:
Yeah, restart policies help. But here's the real answer:

When a pod crashes, Kubernetes doesn't just restart it randomly. It uses an exponential backoff.

First crash? Restart right away.
Second crash? Wait 10 seconds, then restart.
Third? Wait 20 seconds.
Max wait is 5 minutes.

This prevents hammering your system if the pod keeps failing.

BUT — and this is what gets people — you also need:

1. Liveness probes: Tells Kube 'is this pod actually alive?'
2. Readiness probes: Tells Kube 'is this pod ready for traffic?'
3. Resource requests/limits: So a broken pod doesn't eat all your CPU

Real example: Your app crashes every 2 seconds. Without these checks, Kube keeps spinning up new pods. Your cluster melts down.

With probes? Kube stops sending traffic, waits longer between restarts, and gives you time to fix it.

hook: Interviewer: 'What's the difference between a Deployment and a StatefulSet?' — This one trips up so many engineers. Thread 👇
thread:
OK so here's the thing:

A Deployment is for apps that don't care about order. Like a web server. You need 3 copies running? Kubernetes spins up 3 identical pods. If one dies, it just makes another. Order doesn't matter.

A StatefulSet is for apps that DO care about order. Think databases or messaging systems. Each pod gets a stable name (like db-0, db-1, db-2) and its own storage. Pods start and stop in order. Pod 1 comes up first, then Pod 2, then Pod 3.

Real example: You're running a database cluster. You need Pod 0 to be the leader first. With StatefulSet, that happens. With Deployment, pods might start randomly — total chaos.

Bonus tip: StatefulSets are harder to manage. Use Deployments when you can. Only reach for StatefulSet when your app actually needs it.

hook: Interviewer: 'How does Route53 handle failover?' — Most engineers get this wrong. Would you? 👇
thread:

Failover means: if your main server dies, Route53 automatically points traffic to a backup server instead.

1. You set up health checks. Route53 pings your servers every 30 seconds.

2. If a server stops responding, it's marked as "unhealthy."

3. Route53 stops sending traffic there and sends it to your backup instead.

Common mistake: Thinking Route53 fixes the broken server. Nope. It just redirects traffic around it.

Real example:
You have a website on Server A (main) and Server B (backup). Route53 checks Server A every 30 seconds. It dies. Route53 sees no response. Boom — all new visitors go to Server B. Your site stays up.

Let's say you have 3 teams:

• Frontend devs — need to push to your container registry
• Backend devs — need database access too
• DevOps team — needs everything

Don't give frontend devs database access. Don't give backend devs power to delete databases. Give each team a role with only what they need.

In AWS or GCP, this means:
- Create roles (frontend-dev, backend-dev, devops-admin)
- Add specific permissions to each role
- Assign people to roles, not permissions directly

It's called "least privilege." It's the golden rule.

thread:

ArgoCD is about DEPLOYING it. It watches your git repo and says: 'Hey, what's in git should match what's running.' If it doesn't match, ArgoCD fixes it.

CI/CD pipeline = build & test code
ArgoCD = keep deployed stuff in sync with git

They work together, not instead of each other. Your CI/CD builds the image. ArgoCD deploys it.

The magic part? If someone manually changes production (bad idea btw), ArgoCD sees the drift and pulls everything back to what git says. It's like version control for your actual running apps.

hook: Interviewer: 'When would you use Lambda over containers?' — Most candidates get this wrong. Here's what they miss 👇
thread:
Lambda is for SHORT tasks. Containers are for LONG-RUNNING apps. Big difference.

Lambda:
- You write code, AWS runs it
- Pays only when it runs (milliseconds)
- Great for: processing files, handling webhooks, scheduled jobs
- Bad for: 24/7 apps, complex networking

- You control the whole thing
- Pays even when idle
- Great for: APIs running all day, databases, anything needing persistent state
- Bad for: occasional tasks (too expensive)

hook: Interviewer: 'What's the difference between monitoring and observability?' — Most candidates mix these up. Would you? 👇

Monitoring watches known things. You set alerts: 'CPU > 80%, page load > 2 seconds.' You already know what to look for.

Example: Monitoring says 'database is slow.' Observability tells you 'database is slow because this specific query is doing a full table scan on 500k rows.'

hook: Interviewer: 'How would you prevent bad deployments?' — Most candidates miss the actual answer. Thread 👇
thread:
They'll say 'use linting' or 'add tests.' Right, but they're asking about POLICY enforcement.

That's where OPA (Open Policy Agent) comes in.

OPA lets you write rules that block deployments BEFORE they happen. Think of it like a bouncer at the door.

Real example:
- Dev tries to deploy a container with no resource limits
- OPA rule checks: 'Does this have CPU + memory set?'
- If no? Deployment gets blocked. Done.

No resource limits = your pod eats all the server. Bad.

OPA rules are written in a language called Rego. Looks weird at first, but it's just: "if this condition is true, deny the request."

You can use OPA with Kubernetes (via admission controllers), Terraform, or even CI/CD pipelines.

Key wins:
- Catch bad config EARLY (before it reaches prod)
- Same rules everywhere (Kubernetes, Terraform, etc.)
- Teams can't bypass it (it's enforced at the platform level)

Common OPA policies:
- Must have resource requests/limits
- Only certain image registries allowed
- Containers must run as non-root
- Storage must be encrypted

If they ask this in your interview, mention OPA + one specific policy example. You'll stand out.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you deploy to AWS from GitHub Actions?' — Most people wing this. Here's what they miss 👇

The mistake: People think it's just adding a workflow file. Nope.

1. IAM Role Setup
You need an AWS IAM role with the right permissions. GitHub Actions uses OIDC (fancy word for "trusted connection") to talk to AWS without storing secret keys in your repo.

Bad: Hardcoding AWS access keys in GitHub secrets
Good: Using OIDC to assume a role temporarily

2. The Workflow File
Your GitHub Actions workflow runs a job that says: "Hey AWS, it's me (GitHub), can I borrow a temp key?"

Then it deploys. EC2, S3, Lambda, whatever.

3. Real Example

name: Deploy to AWS
on: [push]
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      id-token: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v2
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/github-role
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - run: aws s3 cp app.zip s3://my-bucket/


The key part: `role-to-assume`. That's the trust.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you monitor a Kubernetes cluster?' — Most say Prometheus. But do you know WHY? 👇
thread:
Here's the thing: Prometheus is just a tool that collects numbers about your cluster.

It scrapes metrics (CPU, memory, pod crashes) from your nodes and pods. Then it stores them so you can look back and see what went wrong.

Why Prometheus specifically?

hook: Interviewer: 'What's a Kubernetes StatefulSet and when would you use it instead of a Deployment?' — This trips up way more people than it should 👇
thread:
StatefulSet vs Deployment. Here's the deal:

A Deployment is for apps that don't care about identity. Like a web server. You can spin up 5 copies and they're all the same. If one dies, a new one pops up. Order doesn't matter.

A StatefulSet is for apps that DO care about identity. Think databases, message queues, caches. Each pod gets a sticky name (like "db-0", "db-1", "db-2"). They stay the same even if a pod restarts. Plus they get ordered startup and shutdown.

Example: You're running a database. You can't just spin up a random copy and pretend it's the same as the one that crashed. The new pod needs to sync data, catch up with the others. StatefulSet handles that.

Also: StatefulSets use PersistentVolumes. Each pod gets its own storage that sticks around. A Deployment's storage is temporary.

Quick rule: If your app has state, data, or cares about pod names — StatefulSet. If it's stateless and replaceable — Deployment.

hook: Interviewer: 'How would you use Route53 for failover?' — Most people just say 'health checks' and freeze. Here's the real answer 👇
thread:
Route53 is AWS's DNS service. It points your domain to servers. The failover part is the tricky bit.

Here's what actually happens:

1. You set up a PRIMARY server (main one)
2. You set up a SECONDARY server (backup)
3. Route53 does health checks on the primary every 30 seconds
4. If primary is DOWN, Route53 flips traffic to secondary
5. When primary comes back up, traffic goes back

The key thing most people miss: you need to tell Route53 HOW to check if a server is healthy. Don't just assume it knows.

Example: Your app lives on server A. You tell Route53 "check if server A responds to a health check request every 30 seconds." If it doesn't answer 3 times in a row, Route53 sends all traffic to server B instead.

That's it. It's not magic—it's just automated DNS switching based on health status.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you handle pod crashes in Kubernetes?' — Most candidates miss the real answer. What would you say? 👇
thread:
Here's what they're actually asking: When a pod dies, what happens next?

Wrong answer: "It just... stops?"

Right answer: "Kubernetes notices the pod is dead. It checks the restart policy. Then it spins up a new one automatically."

The key detail most miss: You need to tell Kubernetes HOW to restart things.

Example:
- RestartPolicy: Always (default) = start it again, even if it crashed
- RestartPolicy: OnFailure = only restart if it failed, not if you stopped it
- RestartPolicy: Never = don't restart

Bonus tip: If a pod keeps crashing, Kubernetes adds a delay between restarts. First restart is quick. Second takes longer. This is called exponential backoff — it stops your app from hammering a broken resource.

Think of it like a circuit breaker. Pod crashes → wait a sec → try again → crashes again → wait longer → try again.

One more thing: This is different from SQS or message queues. Those handle app-level retries. Kubernetes handles container-level crashes. Both matter.

hook: Interviewer: 'How does traffic get routed to your containers?' — Most say 'load balancer' and stop there. Here's what they miss 👇

Traffic flow in Kubernetes is actually 3 layers, not 1.

1) INGRESS: Your API Gateway (or Ingress controller) sits outside the cluster. It's the front door. Routes HTTP/HTTPS requests.

2) SERVICE: Inside the cluster, a Service is like a virtual IP. It finds all your Pods running the same app. Spreads traffic across them.

3) ENDPOINTS: The Service watches Pods. When a Pod dies, the Service stops sending traffic there. New Pod? It gets traffic automatically.

You deploy 3 Pods of your API. Service gives them ONE virtual IP. Client hits that IP once. Service picks a random Pod. Client hits it again. Service picks a different Pod. Boom — load balanced.

The tricky part? Engineers forget the Ingress layer. They think Service alone routes external traffic. Wrong. Service is only for internal cluster traffic.

For external traffic, you need an Ingress controller (like NGINX). It watches your Ingress resources and actually creates load balancers.

hook: Interviewer: 'What's the difference between ECS and Fargate?' — Most candidates mix these up. Would you nail it? 👇
thread:
Here's the simple version:

ECS = You manage the servers. You pick the machines. You handle updates. More work, more control.

Fargate = AWS manages the servers for you. You just say 'run my container.' Less work, less control.

Real example:

With ECS on EC2: You spin up 3 servers, tell ECS to run your app on them, patch those servers, pay for idle time.

With Fargate: You just say 'run this container,' Fargate picks the hardware, handles it all. You only pay for what you use.

Catch: Fargate costs more per hour. But if your traffic changes a lot, you save money because you don't pay for idle servers.

When to pick each:
- Fargate = Small team, simple apps, can't handle ops
- ECS on EC2 = Big company, lots of control needed, predictable load

Tbh, most startups go Fargate first. Less headache.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you expose a Kubernetes service outside the cluster?' — Most say Ingress. But there's more to it. 👇
thread:
Here's the thing: there are actually 4 ways to expose a service. Let me break them down.

1. ClusterIP — Only works inside the cluster. Default type. Good for apps talking to each other.

2. NodePort — Opens a port on every node. Anyone outside can hit that port. Simple but messy for production.

3. LoadBalancer — Works with cloud providers like AWS. Creates an actual load balancer in front of your nodes. Your cloud bill goes up though lol.

4. Ingress — This is what people think of first. But Ingress is NOT a service type. It's a separate thing that routes HTTP traffic to services. You still need a service under it.

Real example: You're running a web app. You'd use ClusterIP for the service, then an Ingress to route traffic from the internet to that service. The Ingress controller (like NGINX) handles the actual routing.

Most candidates skip the difference between Ingress and LoadBalancer. That's the trick question.

hook: Interviewer: 'How does Cilium handle network policy differently than Calico?' — Most candidates mix them up. Would you know the answer? 👇
thread:
Here's the key difference:

Calico uses iptables rules. It works at the Linux kernel level but gets slow when you have tons of rules.

Cilium uses eBPF. That's a special tech that runs inside the kernel itself. Way faster. Way more flexible.

Real example:
Say you need to block traffic between two namespaces. With Calico, your server has to check each packet against many iptables rules. Slower.

With Cilium, eBPF programs run directly in the kernel. The packet gets checked once, fast. Plus Cilium can see layer 7 stuff (like API calls) that Calico can't.

Why does this matter in an interview?
They want to know you get that Cilium is newer and more powerful. But also that Calico is still solid for simpler setups.

Bonus: Cilium also handles service mesh stuff out of the box. Calico... not so much.

hook: Interviewer: 'What's a buildpack and why would you use one?' — Most candidates mix it up with Docker. Here's the real answer 👇

2. Your CI tool pulls secrets at runtime, NOT from code
3. Never print secrets in logs
4. Rotate them regularly

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you scale pods based on custom metrics?' — Most candidates say 'HPA' and stop. But KEDA changes the game. 👇
thread:
Here's the thing:

HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) only watches CPU and memory. That's it. So if you need to scale based on queue depth, HTTP requests per second, or database connections? HPA can't do it.

That's where KEDA comes in.

KEDA = Kubernetes Event Autoscaler. It lets you scale pods based on whatever metric you want.

Real example:
Your app processes messages from a queue. When there are 100 messages waiting, spin up 5 pods. When the queue is empty, scale down to 1.

HPA can't do that. KEDA can.

How it works:
1. KEDA watches your queue (or any event source)
2. It reads the queue depth metric
3. It tells Kubernetes: 'Hey, we need 5 pods'
4. Kubernetes scales accordingly

Bonus: KEDA supports 50+ scalers. Kafka, AWS SQS, Prometheus, Redis, etc.

So in an interview, if they ask about custom scaling, mention:
- HPA for CPU/memory only
- KEDA for everything else

That's it. You'll sound like you know what you're doing.

hook: Interviewer: 'How would you stop a bad deployment from reaching prod?' — Most say 'use CI/CD.' That's not the answer they want. 👇
thread:
They're looking for policy enforcement. This is where OPA (Open Policy Agent) comes in.

OPA lets you write rules that block deployments automatically. No humans needed.

Here's the idea:

1. Developer pushes code
2. CI pipeline runs tests
3. OPA checks the code against your rules
4. If it breaks a rule? The build stops. Dead.

Example rule: "No containers running as root." If someone tries it, OPA rejects it before it ships.

You write these rules in a language called Rego. Looks like:

if container_user == "root" {
  deny this deployment
}

It's that simple. OPA integrates with Kubernetes, Docker, Terraform, Jenkins—basically everything.

Why companies love it: You can enforce security, cost, and compliance rules without touching code. One rule stops bad stuff everywhere.

hook: Interviewer: 'Explain a VPC to someone who's never heard of it.' — Most engineers overcomplicate this. You? 👇

Think of it like this: AWS is a huge apartment building. A VPC is your own apartment. You get to decide:

• Who can visit (security groups)
• Which rooms connect (subnets)
• What's locked (network ACLs)

Without a VPC, your databases and servers are on the public floor. Anyone could walk in.

With a VPC, you lock your door. You only let in the traffic YOU allow.

"A VPC keeps my app and data private. I control what gets in and out." That's enough.

Then if they ask deeper, you say: "I'd use public subnets for load balancers, private subnets for databases. That way bad actors can't hit the database directly."

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you set up Prometheus to scrape metrics?' — Most candidates overthink this. Here's what they miss 👇
thread:
Prometheus is just a tool that pulls data from your apps and stores it.

Here's the real flow:

1. Your app exposes metrics on a /metrics endpoint (like port 9090)
2. Prometheus config file (prometheus.yml) tells it WHAT to scrape and WHERE
3. Prometheus hits that endpoint every 15 seconds (or whatever interval you set)
4. It grabs the data and stores it

That's it. No magic.

Quick example:

global:
  scrape_interval: 15s
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'my-app'
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['localhost:9090']


When they ask "how would you make sure it works?" — just go hit the endpoint yourself. curl localhost:9090/metrics. If you see numbers, Prometheus will too.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you manage Terraform state in a team?' — Most candidates say 'remote backend' and stop. Here's what actually matters 👇
thread:
Remote backend is just step one. Here's what actually matters:

**The Real Problem:**
If two engineers run terraform apply at the same time, things break. State gets corrupted. Deployments fail.

**The Answer They Want:**
1. Use remote state (S3, Azure, Terraform Cloud)
2. Enable state locking so only one person can change it at a time
3. Use workspaces or separate folders so staging and prod don't fight
4. Set up version control (git) for your .tf files, NOT for state files

**Real Example:**
You're using Terraform Cloud. Engineer A runs apply. It locks the state. Engineer B tries to apply and has to wait. When A finishes, lock releases. B can now apply safely.

This is why ArgoCD + Terraform works great together — ArgoCD pulls from git, Terraform handles the state locking. No manual conflicts.

**The Mistake:**
Don't store state in git. Ever. It has secrets in it.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you manage state when multiple people run Terraform on the same EKS cluster?' — This one trips up a lot of people 👇
thread:
Most engineers say "just don't do it" lol. But that's not real life.

Here's the actual answer:

You need remote state + locking.

1. Store your state file in S3 (not local)
2. Enable DynamoDB for state locking
3. All Terraform runs lock the same resource

Why? If two people run terraform apply at the same time, they'll step on each other. Remote locking makes sure only one person can change things at a time.

Example setup:
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket = "my-tf-state"
    key = "eks/terraform.tfstate"
    dynamodb_table = "terraform-locks"
  }
}

Bonus: Use workspaces if you need dev/prod separation. But most teams use separate state files instead.

Ngl, this question is about showing you know production reality isn't chaos. You think ahead about how a team actually works.

hook: Interviewer: 'What's the difference between Karpenter and Cluster Autoscaler?' — Most people mix these up. Do you know? 👇
thread:
Both add nodes when your pods need space. But here's the difference:

Cluster Autoscaler: Watches pods that can't fit. Then tells your cloud provider to add a node. Slow. Takes minutes sometimes.

Karpenter: Smarter. Launches nodes in seconds. Picks the cheapest node type for your workload. Removes nodes faster when you don't need them.

Real example: You need 10 new pods fast.

Cluster Autoscaler waits, checks, then requests one big node. Your pods wait.

Karpenter: Spins up the right-sized node in 20 seconds. Your pods run now.

Karpenter also consolidates better. If you have 5 half-full nodes, it packs them into 3 and removes the extras. Saves money.

The catch? Karpenter is newer. Not all teams use it yet. And it only works with AWS, Azure, GCP (different versions).

Cluster Autoscaler works everywhere.

So in interviews, they want to know: Do you get that Karpenter is faster AND cheaper? That's the key difference.

hook: Interviewer: 'How is KEDA different from HPA?' — Most candidates mix them up. Would you? 👇
thread:
HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) scales based on CPU or memory only.

KEDA (Kubernetes Event Driven Autoscaling) scales based on... anything. AWS queues, Kafka topics, HTTP endpoints, database metrics.

Real example:
→ HPA: 'Spin up more pods when CPU hits 80%'
→ KEDA: 'Spin up more pods when there are 100 messages in my SQS queue'

KEDA is event-driven. HPA is metric-driven. That's the main difference.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do Kubernetes pods talk to each other across nodes?' — Most people get this wrong. Here's what they miss 👇
thread:
OK so here's the thing. Pods on the same node? They just talk directly. Easy.

But pods on DIFFERENT nodes? That's where people mess up.

Kubernetes gives each pod its own IP address. When a pod on Node A talks to a pod on Node B, the network has to route that traffic.

Here's the key: Kubernetes needs a network plugin (called a CNI) to handle this. It sets up routes so traffic finds the right pod, even across nodes.

In AWS? You'd use something like the VPC CNI plugin. It makes sure pods on different EC2 instances can reach each other using AWS VPC networking.

TLDR: Pods get IPs → CNI plugin routes traffic between nodes → pods talk to each other. Done.

hook: Interviewer: 'When would you use SNS over SQS?' — Most engineers get this wrong. Here's the real answer 👇
thread:
SNS and SQS do different jobs. Don't mix them up.

SNS = broadcast. One message goes to MANY places at once. Like a megaphone.

SQS = queue. One message goes to ONE worker. That worker picks it up when ready. Like a mailbox.

Real example:
- SNS: "New user signed up!" → Tell email service, billing, analytics all at once
- SQS: "Process payment" → Put it in a queue. One payment worker grabs it, processes, moves on.

Here's the trick: You can actually use BOTH together. SNS publishes → SQS queues receive. Now each service gets the message at its own pace without losing it.

When they ask this, just say:
"SQS for one-to-one work. SNS for one-to-many notifications. Use them together when you need reliability + speed."

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you manage CloudFront cache invalidation in Terraform?' — Most candidates get this wrong. 👇

You need to tell CloudFront "hey, this stuff is old, grab it again."

Two ways to do it in Terraform:

1. **Manual invalidation** — Use aws_cloudfront_invalidation resource. You specify which files to refresh (like /* for everything).

2. **Auto-invalidate with etag** — Hash your files and let Terraform trigger invalidation when files actually change.

Example that actually works:

aws_cloudfront_invalidation {
  distribution_id = aws_cloudfront_distribution.my_site.id
  paths = ["/index.html", "/*"]
}

Tip: Don't invalidate EVERYTHING every time. It costs money and slows down your users. Only invalidate what changed.

hook: Interviewer: 'What's the difference between HPA and KEDA?' — Most candidates mix these up. Would you? 👇
thread:
Great question. They both scale your apps, but in different ways.

HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) watches CPU and memory. When your pods use too much, it spins up more copies. Super simple.

KEDA (Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling) is smarter. It scales based on real events — like messages in a queue, HTTP requests per second, or database load.

REAL EXAMPLE:
- HPA: "Your app uses 80% CPU, add more pods"
- KEDA: "There are 50 messages waiting in RabbitMQ, add 5 pods to process them faster"

KEDA wins when you care about actual work, not just resources. Perfect for jobs, queues, and event-driven stuff.

Pro tip: You can use both together. HPA handles general load. KEDA handles specific events.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you know who deleted that S3 bucket?' — Most candidates panic. Here's what they miss 👇

Real example: You see a DeleteBucket call at 3 AM from an old IP. Red flag. Probably a security issue.

Bonus tip: Enable CloudTrail logging for ALL regions. Not just one. People miss this.

Also: CloudTrail data goes to S3. But by default it only keeps 90 days. If you need longer history, set up S3 storage.

hook: Interviewer: 'What's the difference between EventBridge and SQS?' — Most candidates mix these up. Would you nail it? 👇
thread:
Here's the thing: they're both AWS services, but they do different jobs.

SQS is a message queue. You throw messages in. Workers pull them out one at a time. It's simple and reliable.

EventBridge is an event router. You send events from different sources. Rules match the events. Then they get sent to the right place.

Real example:

SQS: "Customer ordered something." Workers process orders one by one.

EventBridge: "Customer ordered something." Now you want to trigger notifications, update inventory, log it, AND send it to your data team. EventBridge routes that one event to all those places at once.

The key? EventBridge handles complex routing. SQS handles simple queuing. EventBridge is better when you need multiple things to happen from one event.

hook: Interviewer: 'What's the difference between OPA and a network policy?' — Most engineers mix these up. Here's what they miss 👇
thread:
OPA and network policies do different jobs. Don't confuse them.

Network Policy = stops traffic between pods. That's it. Port level stuff.

OPA (Open Policy Agent) = says yes or no to ANY decision. Can it access this? Can it deploy this? Can it read that secret?

Real example:

Network Policy blocks Pod A from talking to Pod B on port 5432. Good.

But Pod A could still TRY to connect 100 times. OPA can say: "Nope, Pod A isn't allowed to even REQUEST that connection." It catches it earlier.

Another one: You deploy a container image. Network Policy doesn't care. OPA can block it because the image isn't from your trusted registry.

So here's the trick: Use Network Policy for traffic control. Use OPA for permission gates BEFORE things happen.

They work together, but they're not the same thing.

hook: Interviewer: 'Why would you put CloudFront in front of your app?' — Most candidates say 'speed' and stop there. Here's what they miss 👇

1. It's not just for speed. It's also a shield. Stops bad traffic before it hits your app.

2. You can cache smart. "Hey CloudFront, keep this for 1 hour, refresh that every minute."

3. It saves your wallet. Less traffic = less load on your servers = lower bills.

Real example: You're running a video site. New video drops. 100k people want it. Without CloudFront? Your server gets crushed. With it? CloudFront spreads the load across the world. Your app just chills.

One more thing: CloudFront can compress images, block countries, and even run code at the edge (close to users) before they hit your app.

hook: Interviewer: 'How would you debug a slow request in Istio?' — Most candidates struggle here. What's your move? 👇
thread:
Here's the real answer:

Istio sits between your apps. It watches traffic. When something's slow, you check THREE things:

1) SERVICE MESH METRICS
Check how long requests sit in Istio's proxy. Use Prometheus. Look for "istio_request_duration_milliseconds". High? Istio's the bottleneck.

2) DISTRIBUTED TRACING
Use Jaeger or Zipkin. Trace follows your request through every service. You see exactly where it slows down. Is it your app? Or waiting on another service?

3) LOGS + POD METRICS
Check if your pods are overloaded. CPU? Memory? Network? Istio can't fix a broken app.

REAL TIP: Start with tracing first. It's the fastest way to spot the culprit. Then drill into metrics.

Most engineers skip tracing and guess. That's the mistake.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you know if your container is actually healthy?' — Most say 'it's running.' That's wrong. 👇
thread:
Health checks are WAY more than just 'is the process alive.'

A container can be running but broken. Your app might be stuck in a loop. The database connection hung. The API is timing out.

That's where health checks come in. They're your early warning system.

**Here's how:**

1. **Liveness probe** — Is my app still alive? If not, kill it and start fresh.

2. **Readiness probe** — Is my app ready to handle traffic? Don't send requests to it if it's still warming up.

**Real example:**
You're running a Node app. Just because the process started doesn't mean it finished connecting to the database.

Your health check hits an endpoint like /health that checks:
- Can I talk to the database?
- Is my cache working?
- Am I overloaded?

If any of those fail, you tell Kubernetes "don't send me traffic yet" or "restart me."

Without this? Your app looks fine but users get errors.

hook: Interviewer: 'Walk me through how you'd secure a config file with secrets.' — Most engineers mess this up. Would you? 👇

What TO do instead:

3. Rotate secrets regularly. If a secret leaks, change it everywhere.

Real example: Your Kubernetes pod needs a database password. Don't write it in your config file. Instead, create a Kubernetes Secret object. Mount it in your pod. Your app reads it from a mounted file or env var. The secret stays encrypted in Kubernetes.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you secure traffic between pods in EKS?' — Most candidates freeze. Here's what they miss 👇
thread:
The trap: saying 'use a firewall' or 'network policies' without explaining HOW.

Here's the real answer:

Pods talk to each other inside your cluster by default. No auth. Anyone can listen.

You need THREE things:

1. NETWORK POLICIES — Think of them like firewall rules but for pods. You write YAML that says 'Pod A can talk to Pod B, but Pod C cannot.' EKS uses something called Calico or Cilium to actually enforce these.

2. SERVICE MESH (optional) — Tools like Istio add encryption + auth at the container level. Every pod gets a certificate. Pods check each other's certs before talking.

3. mTLS (mutual TLS) — Both sides prove who they are before sharing data. "Hey, I'm Pod A with certificate X." "Okay, I'm Pod B with certificate Y. Let's talk."

Real example:
- You have a web pod and a database pod
- Without network policies, anyone in the cluster can hit your database
- With policies, only the web pod's IP range can reach port 5432
- With mTLS, the database pod also checks that the web pod has a valid cert

Most interviews just want to hear: 'I'd use network policies to block bad traffic, then layer on mTLS for extra security.'

1. COLLECT metrics (Prometheus)
2. VISUALIZE them (Grafana)

hook: Interviewer: 'What's the difference between SNS and SQS?' — Most engineers fumble this. Would you nail it? 👇
thread:
SNS = someone yelling in a room. Everyone in the room hears it. SQS = a mailbox. Messages sit there until someone picks them up.

SNS is PUSH. It sends your message right now to whoever's subscribed.

SQS is PULL. Your app grabs messages when it's ready.

Real example:

You run an online store. Order placed → SNS fires → your email service, SMS service, and analytics all get the event at the same time. They don't wait. That's SNS.

But what if your SMS service is slow or down? SNS already sent it. The message might get lost.

With SQS, your workers can grab orders one at a time from the queue. If one crashes, the message stays in the queue. Another worker picks it up later. More reliable for critical stuff.

Quick tip: Use SNS when speed matters and you have multiple subscribers. Use SQS when you need a buffer between services.

✅ Flux: Your Git repo is the source of truth. Flux keeps your cluster in sync with it.

Flux also catches drift. If someone manually deletes a pod, Flux notices and fixes it. Your repo is always the real state.

That's the key: Git as the single source of truth. Helm is just a tool to package and install. Flux is the automation.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you update a ConfigMap without restarting your pods?' — Most candidates get this wrong. 👇
thread:
Here's the thing: just changing a ConfigMap doesn't magically update your running pods. Your app won't see the new values unless you reload it.

Three ways to handle this:

1. RESTART THE POD (easiest)
Delete your pod. Kubernetes spins up a new one. It reads the fresh ConfigMap. Done.

2. USE A SIDECAR (clever)
Run a small container that watches the ConfigMap. When it changes, the sidecar tells your app to reload config. No restart needed.

3. BUILD IT INTO YOUR APP (best long-term)
Make your app check for config changes every X seconds. It reloads automatically. No DevOps magic needed.

For interviews, say option 1 first (it's honest and simple). Then mention you'd use option 3 in production so your app doesn't have hard stops.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you handle CloudFormation stack updates without downtime?' — Most engineers panic here. Thread 👇
thread:
Here's the real talk:

CloudFormation tries to update resources in place. Sometimes that works. Sometimes it breaks everything.

When it breaks? You get a rollback. Your whole stack goes back to how it was.

To avoid downtime, you need a strategy:

1. **Blue-green deploys** — Keep two stacks running. Switch traffic to the new one when it's ready. If it fails, switch back.

2. **Update policies** — Tell CloudFormation to create a new resource BEFORE deleting the old one. Keeps your app online during the swap.

3. **Stack policies** — Lock down which resources can change. Prevents accidental updates to critical stuff.

Real example: You're updating an EC2 instance. If CloudFormation has to replace it (not just update it), your app goes down. With a blue-green approach? You spin up a new instance, test it, then switch over. Zero downtime.

The key: Plan for failures. Always assume something will break.

hook: Interviewer: 'Walk me through your VPC setup in Terraform' — Most engineers fumble this. Would you? 👇
thread:
Here's how to nail it:

Start simple. A VPC is just a network space in AWS. In Terraform, you define it like this:

resource "aws_vpc" "main" {
  cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16"
}

Then add subnets (smaller chunks inside your VPC). Public subnets get internet access. Private ones don't.

Next, mention an internet gateway. That's what lets your public subnet talk to the outside world.

Then talk about route tables. They're like GPS for your network traffic. "If traffic goes here, send it there."

Real tip: In interviews, draw this out or describe it step by step. Don't just code dump. Show you understand WHAT each piece does, not just HOW to write it.

Say something like: "I'd create a VPC, add a public subnet for my web servers, a private subnet for my database, then set up routing so traffic flows right."

hook: Interviewer: 'What's a buildpack and why would you use one?' — Most candidates confuse it with Docker. Here's what you need to know 👇
thread:
A buildpack is just a tool that takes your code and builds it into a container image. No Dockerfile needed.

Think of it like this:
- You push your code
- Buildpack detects what language it is (Node, Python, Java, etc)
- It automatically installs dependencies
- Creates a working container

Why use it? Speed and consistency. You don't write a Dockerfile. The buildpack handles everything.

Real example: Heroku uses buildpacks. You git push your Node app, Heroku's buildpack runs, detects package.json, installs npm packages, sets up the runtime. Done.

Key difference from Docker: With Docker you write exact steps. With buildpacks? They figure it out.

When would you pick buildpacks? When you want fast deployments and don't want to maintain Dockerfiles. When you want less configuration.

hook: Interviewer: 'What's the difference between a container and a VM?' — Most engineers fumble this one. Here's the real answer 👇
thread:
A VM is a fake computer. It pretends to be a whole machine with its own OS, disk, memory — everything.

A container is just your app + what it needs to run. It shares the real computer's OS with other containers.

Why it matters:

VMs = slower, bigger, use way more resources
Containers = fast, small, you can run 100 on one machine

Real example:
If you need to run Python 3.11, a database, and a web server:

🔴 VM way: Install 3 full operating systems. Each one takes 5GB+ of disk.

🟢 Container way: Pack them each in their own box. Total size: maybe 500MB. They all share the same Linux kernel underneath.

That's why Docker is so popular. It made containers dead simple to use.

Bit of a bonus: VMs are more locked down (better security isolation). Containers are lighter but all share the OS, so one bad app can hurt others. But in practice? Containers win for speed and cost.

hook: Interviewer: 'What's the difference between CDK and CloudFormation?' — Most engineers mix these up. Would you? 👇
thread:
Here's the thing: CloudFormation is the old way. You write YAML or JSON. It's like writing a recipe by hand.

CDK is newer. You write actual code. Python, TypeScript, whatever. Then it turns into CloudFormation behind the scenes.

Real example:

CloudFormation:

Resources:
  MyBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      BucketName: my-bucket


CDK (TypeScript):

const bucket = new s3.Bucket(this, 'MyBucket', {
  bucketName: 'my-bucket'
});


Same result. But CDK is way easier to read and reuse.

Why pick CDK? You get loops, functions, variables. You can write actual logic. No more copy-pasting YAML.

Why stick with CloudFormation? Smaller projects. Less moving parts. Your team knows it.

Pro tip: CDK still generates CloudFormation. So they work together. Not enemies.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you handle DynamoDB hot partitions?' — Most candidates panic here. Would you know what to say? 👇
thread:
A hot partition is when all your traffic hits one part of DynamoDB at once. Think of it like everyone in a store lining up at one checkout.

What happens? You hit your throughput limit. Your app slows down. Users get mad.

How to fix it:

1. Add a random number to your key — spreads the load across partitions
2. Use DynamoDB Streams — read the hot data separately 
3. Cache it with ElastiCache — stop hitting DynamoDB so much
4. Design better keys from the start — don't use timestamps as your main key if everyone's writing to "today"

Real example: You're logging events. If your key is just the date, all writes go to the same partition on that day. Bad.

Instead: date + random(1-100). Now writes spread across 100 partitions. Problem solved.

Biggest mistake? Waiting until production to find this out.

hook: Interviewer: 'How would you cache a website using CloudFront?' — Most engineers overthink this. Here's what they miss 👇
thread:
CloudFront is just a CDN. Sounds fancy, but it's simple:

1. Your website sits in an origin (like S3 or your server)
2. CloudFront copies your stuff to servers around the world
3. Users get your content from the closest server. Fast.

That's it.

In an interview, they want to hear:
- Set up an origin (S3 bucket)
- Create a CloudFront distribution pointing to it
- Set cache rules (what to cache, how long)
- Users now load faster because they're not always hitting your main server

Real example: Say you host a photo app. Without CloudFront, everyone downloads from one place. With it? Photos come from a server near them. 50ms instead of 500ms.

Common miss: Engineers say "I'll cache everything forever." Wrong. Cache images for days. Cache HTML for minutes. Cache API calls? Usually don't.

That's the answer they're looking for. Simple and practical.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you keep your secrets safe in the cloud?' — Most candidates get this wrong. Here's what they miss 👇
thread:
Secrets are things like passwords, API keys, database creds. You can't just hardcode them in your app or commit them to git.

Best practice? Use a secrets manager like AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault.

Here's how it works:

1. Store your secrets in the manager
2. Your app asks for the secret when it starts
3. The manager gives it to your app (not stored locally)
4. If the secret changes, you update it once—no redeploying

Why this matters:
- If someone gets your code, they don't get passwords
- You can rotate secrets without stopping your app
- You can audit who accessed what
- Different apps can have different secrets

One more thing: KMS (Key Management Service) is usually paired with this. KMS encrypts the secrets so even AWS can't read them without your permission. It's like a safe inside a safe.

Real example: Production database password lives in Secrets Manager, encrypted by KMS. Your Lambda function grabs it at runtime. Clean and secure.

hook: Interviewer: 'What's Crossplane?' — Most candidates say 'infrastructure tool' and stop there. Here's what they miss 👇
thread:
Crossplane lets you manage cloud stuff using Kubernetes. Instead of logging into AWS or Azure, you just write YAML and kubectl apply it.

Why this matters in interviews:

Most people just say "it manages infrastructure." That's true but boring.

The real answer:

Crossplane is a control plane. It watches your YAML files. When you change something, it talks to AWS/Azure/GCP and makes those changes real. It's like having Kubernetes drive your cloud account.

Quick example:
You write a YAML file that says "I want an S3 bucket." Crossplane reads it. Then it actually creates the bucket in AWS. You never touch the AWS console.

Why companies care:

- One tool for everything (Kubernetes)
- You can version control your cloud stuff
- Same workflow for apps AND infrastructure
- Engineers don't need AWS console access

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you handle node failures in EKS?' — Most people just say 'auto scaling.' That's not the full answer 👇
thread:
Here's what they actually want to hear:

When a node dies in EKS, three things happen:

1. Kubernetes notices the node is gone (takes ~40 seconds)
2. It reschedules pods to healthy nodes
3. Auto Scaling Group spins up a new node

BUT — if you don't set pod requests/limits, the new node might be too small. Your pods fail to reschedule. Boom.

The real answer: Use resource requests, set pod disruption budgets, and enable cluster autoscaler. That way when a node fails, your pods move smoothly and a fresh node joins without drama.

Also mention: Spot instances are cheaper but can die anytime. Good for non-critical stuff. Use on-demand for critical apps.

hook: Interviewer: 'Design a CI/CD pipeline for us.' — Most candidates miss the obvious thing. Here's what they should say 👇
thread:
Here's the thing: a good pipeline is like an assembly line. Code comes in one end. A working app comes out the other.

Most people jump straight to tools (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, whatever). But that's backwards.

Start with the STEPS:

1️⃣ Code pushed → run tests
2️⃣ Tests pass → build the app
3️⃣ Build works → deploy to staging
4️⃣ Manual check → deploy to production

Each step blocks the next. If tests fail, don't build. If build fails, don't deploy.

THEN pick your tool. GitHub Actions is great because it's free, simple, and built into GitHub.

The real answer? Describe the FLOW first. The tool is just the thing that runs it.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you manage configs across dev, staging, and prod?' — This trips up most engineers. Here's the right answer 👇
thread:
Most people say 'we use env vars' and stop. That's incomplete.

Here's what they're really asking:

1. HOW do you store configs?
- Use a config management tool (ConfigMap in Kubernetes, Secrets Manager in AWS, etc)
- NOT hardcoded in your app
- NOT in git repos (security risk)

2. HOW do you keep them separate?
- One config per environment
- Load the right one when your app starts
- Example: app checks if NODE_ENV=prod, then loads prod secrets

3. HOW do you update them?
- Change the config, restart the app
- Or use a tool that hot-reloads (fancy but optional)

Real example:
Dev team uses ConfigMap for database URLs. Prod team uses AWS Secrets Manager. Same app code. Different configs. Problem solved.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you manage infrastructure as code?' — Most say CloudFormation. Then they freeze. Here's what they miss 👇
thread:
CloudFormation is just a way to write your AWS setup in a text file instead of clicking around in the console.

BUT here's the thing: A lot of people treat it like a magic wand. They don't understand WHEN it's actually the right tool.

Real talk:

CloudFormation is great when you need to:
— Spin up the same setup 10 times
— Change things and roll back fast
— Share code with your team
— Track who changed what

It sucks when you:
— Need to manage 500+ resources (gets slow)
— Have super custom logic
— Work with other clouds too

The secret? Ask yourself: "Do I need repeatability and version control?" If yes, use it. If you're just testing something quick? Just use the console.

Also, write templates small. Don't dump your whole app in one file. Break it into pieces. Makes updates way less risky.

hook: Interviewer: 'How do you monitor config drift?' — Most SREs mess this up. Here's what they miss 👇
thread:
Config drift = your actual system doesn't match what you wrote down.

Example: You deploy with Terraform. Then someone SSH's in and changes a setting. Now prod is different from your code. Bad.

How to catch it:

1. Check your configs regularly. Don't just deploy once and forget.

2. Use tools that scan. Prometheus scrapes metrics. But you also need config audits. Tools like Ansible or Chef can compare what should be vs what is.

3. Alert when something changes. If a file gets edited, you should know.

4. Version everything. Git repo = single source of truth. Always.

Real tip: Most teams find drift by accident. Mature teams check for it every day. Automated scans beat manual reviews.

The goal: Your code should match your servers. Always. No surprises at 2am.
